indicators.indicatorName: Abnormal Password Refresh
indicators.description: Looks for user accounts with a recent pwdLastSet change without a corresponding password replication. If the “User must change password at next logon” option is set and then later cleared, could indicate an administrative error or an attempt to bypass the organization’s password policy.

indicators.indicatorName: AD objects created within the last 10 days
indicators.description: Looks for any AD objects that were recently created. Allows you to spot unknown or illegitimate accounts. Meant to be used for threat hunting, post-breach investigation, or compromise validation.

indicators.indicatorName: Admins with old passwords
indicators.description: Looks for Admin accounts whose password has not changed in over 180 days. If Admin account passwords are not changed on a regular basis, these accounts could be ripe for password guessing attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Built-in domain Administrator account used within the last two weeks
indicators.description: Checks to see if the lastLogonTimestamp for the built-in Domain Administrator account has been recently updated. Could indicate that the user has been compromised.

indicators.indicatorName: Built-in domain Administrator account with old password (180 days)
indicators.description: Checks to see if the pwdLastSet attribute on the built-in Domain Administrator account has been changed within the last 180 days. If this password is not changed on a regular basis, this account can be vulnerable to brute force password attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to PreWindows 2000 Compatible Access Group membership
indicators.description: Looks for changes to the built-in “Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access” group. It is best to ensure this group does not contain the “Anonymous Logon” or “Everyone” groups.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to privileged group membership in the last 7 days
indicators.description: Looks for recent changes to the built-in-privileged groups. Could indicate attempts to escalate privilege.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to unprivileged group membership in the last 7 days
indicators.description: Looks for unprivileged groups with memberships changes made during the last 7 days. Membership changes to unprivileged groups may give access to resources using group privileges.

indicators.indicatorName: Computer accounts in privileged groups
indicators.description: Looks for computer accounts that are a member of a domain privileged group. If a computer account is a member of the domain privileged group, then anyone that compromises that computer account can act as a member of that group.

indicators.indicatorName: Computers with no password set
indicators.description: Checks for computer objects that did not join the domain and most likely have no password set. In many organizations, automated scripts or legacy tools like “dsadd” are used to pre-create computer accounts. When tools like “dsadd” are used, the computer object is created with a blank (unset) password. This password is intended to remain empty until the actual computer joins the domain. However, if the computer never joins the domain, it remains in a vulnerable state with no password set. Attackers can exploit these pre-created, unused computer accounts for lateral movement and privilege escalation within the domain.

indicators.indicatorName: Distributed COM Users group or Performance Log Users group are not empty
indicators.description: Checks for non-privileged users that cannot complete the MFA process based on the authentication details they enter. MFA adds an extra layer of security to the sign-in process, which helps protect your organization against security breaches. Users who use MFA are less likely to fall victim to phishing attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Enabled admin accounts that are inactive
indicators.description: Looks for admin accounts that are enabled, but have not log in for the past 90 days. Attackers who can compromise these accounts will be able to operate unnoticed.

indicators.indicatorName: Ephemeral Admins
indicators.description: Looks for users that were added and removed from an Admin group within a 48-hour period. Such short-lived accounts may indicate malicious activity.

indicators.indicatorName: FGPP not applied to Group
indicators.description: Looks for fine-grained password policy (FGPP) targeted to a Universal or Domain Local group. Changing a group’s scope setting from Global to Universal or Domain Local, results in FGPP settings no longer applying to that group, thus decreasing its password security controls.

indicators.indicatorName: Forest contains more than 50 privileged accounts
indicators.description: Counts the number of privileged accounts defined in the forest. In general, the more privileged accounts you have, the more opportunities there are for attackers to compromise one of these accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: Operator Groups that are not empty
indicators.description: Looks for operator groups (Account Operators, Server Operators, Backup Operators, Print Operators) that contain members. These groups have write access to critical resources on the domain; attackers that are members of these groups can take indirect control of the domain.

indicators.indicatorName: OU permissions enabling BadSuccessor dMSA escalation
indicators.description: Checks for excessive permissions to create delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSAs) within Active Directory organizational units (OU) or the Naming Context (NC) head across domains that contain Windows Server 2025 domain controllers. The indicator identifies non-privileged identities that have been granted CreateChild, GenericAll, WriteDACL, or WriteOwner permissions on OUs or the NC head, which could enable the execution of the “BadSuccessor” Privilege Escalation attack. The “BadSuccessor” attack is a technique that exploits vulnerabilities in Microsoft’s Active Directory and enables domain takeover leveraging dMSAs.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged accounts with a password that never expires
indicators.description: Identifies privileged accounts (adminCount = 1) where the “Password Never Expires” flag is set. User accounts whose passwords never expire are ripe targets for brute force password guessing. If these accounts are also administrative or privileged accounts, this makes them more of a target.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged users that are disabled
indicators.description: Looks for privileged user accounts that are disabled. If a privileged account is disabled, it should be removed from its privileged group(s) to prevent inadvertent misuse.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged users with weak password policy
indicators.description: Looks for privileged users in each domain that do not have a strong password policy enforced, according to ANSSI framework . It checks both the Fine-Grained Password Policy (FGPP) and the password policy applied to the domain. A strong password defined by ANSSI is at least eight characters long and updated no later than every three years. Weak passwords are easier to crack via brute-force attacks and can provide attackers opportunities for moving laterally or escalating privileges. The risk is even higher for privileged accounts, for when compromised they improve the attacker’s chance to quickly advance within the network.

indicators.indicatorName: Protected Users group not in use
indicators.description: Detects when privileged users are not a member of the Protected Users group. The Protected Users group provides privileged users with additional protection from direct credential theft attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Recent privileged account creation activity
indicators.description: Looks for any privileged users or groups (adminCount = 1) that were recently created. Allows you to spot privileged accounts and groups that were created without prior knowledge. Informational

indicators.indicatorName: Recent sIDHistory changes on objects
indicators.description: Detects any recent changes to the sIDHistory on objects, including changes to non-privileged accounts where privileged SIDs are added. Attackers need privileged access to AD to be able to write to sIDHistory, but if such rights exist then writing privileged SIDs to regular user accounts is a stealthy way of creating backdoor accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: Shadow Credentials on privileged objects
indicators.description: Looks for users with write access to the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute of privileged users and domain controllers. Users who can write to these privileged objects and Kerberos PKINIT is enabled can elevate privileges to these objects.

indicators.indicatorName: Trust accounts with old passwords
indicators.description: Looks for trust accounts whose password has not changed within the last year. Trust accounts facilitate authentication across trusts and should be protected like privileged user accounts. Normally, trust account passwords are rotated automatically, so a trust account without a recent password change could indicate an orphaned trust account.

indicators.indicatorName: Unprivileged accounts with adminCount=1
indicators.description: Looks for any users or groups that may be under the control of SDProp (adminCount=1) but are no longer members of privileged groups. Might be evidence of an attacker that attempted to cover their tracks and remove a user they used for compromise.

indicators.indicatorName: Unprivileged principals as DNS Admins
indicators.description: Looks for any member of the DNS Admins group that is not a privileged user. Members of this group can be delegated to non-AD administrators (e.g. Admins with networking responsibilities, such as DNS, DHCP, etc.), which can result in these accounts being prime targets for compromise.

indicators.indicatorName: User accounts that store passwords with reversible encryption
indicators.description: Identifies accounts with the “ENCRYPTED_TEXT_PWD_ALLOWED” flag enabled. Attackers may be able to derive these users’ passwords from the ciphertext and take over these accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: User accounts that use DES encryption
indicators.description: Identifies user accounts with the “Use Kerberos DES encryption types for this account” flag set. Attackers can easily crack DES passwords using widely available tools, making these accounts ripe for takeover.

indicators.indicatorName: User accounts using Smart Card authentication with old password
indicators.description: Looks for user accounts that are using Smart Card authentication whose password has not changed in the last 90 days. A user may use a Smart Card for authentication instead of a password. By default, accounts with the “Smart Card required” flag enabled have disabled password rotation. This static password hash is used for signing Kerberos tickets, and if compromised, may lead to credential-theft-based attacks such as Silver Ticket attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: User accounts with password not required
indicators.description: Identifies user accounts where a password is not required. Accounts with weak access controls are often targeted to move laterally or gain a persistence foothold with the environment.

indicators.indicatorName: Users and computers with non-default Primary Group IDs
indicators.description: Returns a list of all users and computers whose Primary Group IDs (PGIDs) are not the defaults for domain users and computers. Modifying the Primary Group ID is a stealthy way for an attacker to escalate privileges without triggering member attribute auditing for group membership changes.

indicators.indicatorName: Users and computers without readable PGID
indicators.description: Finds users and computers that can not read the Primary Group ID (PGID). May be caused by removing the default Read permission, which could indicate an attempt to hide the user (in combination with removal of the memberOf attribute).

indicators.indicatorName: Users with Kerberos pre- authentication disabled
indicators.description: Looks for users with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled. These users can be targeted for ASREP-Roasting attacks (like “Kerberoasting”).

indicators.indicatorName: Users with old passwords
indicators.description: Looks for user accounts whose password has not changed in over 180 days. These accounts could be ripe for password guessing attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Users with Password Never Expires flag set
indicators.description: Identifies user accounts where the “Password Never Expires” flag is set. These accounts can be potential targets for brute force password attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Built-in guest account is enabled
indicators.description: Checks to ensure that the built-in AD “guest” account is disabled. An enabled guest account allows for passwordless access to the domain, which could present a security risk.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to AD display specifiers in the past 90 days
indicators.description: Looks for recent changes made to the adminContextMenu attribute on AD display specifiers. Modifying this attribute can potentially allow attackers to utilize context menus to get users to run arbitrary code.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to default security descriptor schema in the last 90 days
indicators.description: Detects recent schema attribute changes made on the default security descriptor. If an attacker gets access to the schema instance in a forest, any changes made can propagate to newly created objects in AD, potentially weakening AD security posture.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to MS LAPS read permissions
indicators.description: Looks for permissions on computer accounts that could allow inadvertent exposure of local administrator accounts in environments that use Microsoft LAPS. Attackers may use this capability to laterally move through a domain using compromised local administrator accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous delegated rights on Active Directory OUs
indicators.description: Identifies Organizational Units (OUs) in Active Directory that have been delegated powerful permissions, which could lead to security risks or unauthorized privilege escalation. Powerful permissions delegated on Organizational Units (OUs) in Active Directory can bypass standard security controls and pose a high risk if assigned inappropriately. This indicator focuses on the Reanimate_Tombstone, Unexpire_Password, and SID_History permissions.

indicators.indicatorName: Domain Controller owner is not an administrator
indicators.description: Looks for Domain Controller computer accounts whose owner is not a Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or built-in Administrator account. Gaining control of DC machine accounts allows for an easy path to compromising the domain.

indicators.indicatorName: Enterprise Key Admins with full access to domain
indicators.description: Looks for evidence of a bug in certain versions of Windows Server 2016 Adprep that granted undue access to the Enterprise Key Admins group. This issue was corrected in a subsequent release of Windows 2016; however, if this fix has not been applied, this bug grants this group the ability to replicate all changes from AD (DCSync attack).

indicators.indicatorName: Foreign Security Principals in Privileged Group
indicators.description: Looks for members of built-in protected groups which are Foreign Security Principals. Special care should be taken when including accounts from other domains as members of privileged groups. Foreign Security Principals do not have the adminCount attribute and therefore may not be detected by some security auditing tools. Additionally, an attacker may add a privileged account and attempt to hide it using this method.

indicators.indicatorName: gMSA not used
indicators.description: Checks for enabled group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) objects in the domain. The gMSA feature in Windows Server 2016 allows automatic rotation of passwords for service accounts, making them much more difficult for attackers to compromise.

indicators.indicatorName: Inheritance enabled on AdminSDHolder object
indicators.description: Checks for inheritance being enabled on the Access Control List (ACL) of the AdminSDHolder object, which could indicate an attempt to modify permissions on privileged objects that are subject to AdminSDHolder (for example, users or groups with adminCount=1). Changes to the AdminSDHolder object are very rare. Administrators should know that a change was made and be able to articulate the reason for the change. If the change was not intentional, the likelihood of compromise is very high.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-default access to DPAPI key
indicators.description: Checks domain controllers for non-default principals that are permitted to retrieve the domain DPAPI backup key(using LsaRetrievePrivateData). With these permissions, an attacker could recover all domain data encrypted via DPAPI.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-default access to gMSA root key
indicators.description: Looks for non-default principals with permissions to read the msKds-RootKeyData attribute on the KDS root key. Users with read permissions to this property could compromise every gMSA account in the forest.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-default principals with DC Sync rights on the domain
indicators.description: Looks for security principals with Replicating Changes All or Replicating Directory Changes permissions on the domain naming context object. Security principals with these permissions on the domain naming context object can potentially retrieve password hashes for users in an AD domain (DCSync attack).

indicators.indicatorName: Non-default value on ms-Mcs-AdmPwd SearchFlags
indicators.description: Looks for changes to the default searchFlags on the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd schema. Some flags may inadvertently cause the password to be visible to unintended users allowing an attacker to use it as a stealthy backdoor.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-privileged users with access to gMSA passwords
indicators.description: Looks for principals listed within the MSDS-groupMSAmembership that are not in the built-in admin groups. An attacker that controls access to the gMSA account can retrieve passwords for resources managed with gMSA.

indicators.indicatorName: Objects in privileged groups without adminCount=1 (SDProp)
indicators.description: Looks for objects in built-in privileged groups whose adminCount attribute is not set to 1. If an object within these groups has an adminCount not equal to 1, they could signify that the DACLs were manually set (no inheritance) or that there is an issue with SDProp.

indicators.indicatorName: Objects with Reanimate-Tombstones extended rights
indicators.description: Checks if there are any non-default principals with the Reanimate-Tombstones extended rights configured. It is recommended to only delegate this right to domain administrators, since tombstone reanimation is an uncommon and highly privileged operation.

indicators.indicatorName: Permission changes on AdminSDHolder object
indicators.description: Looks for Access Control List (ACL) changes on the AdminSDHolder object. Could indicate an attempt to modify permissions on privileged objects that are subject to AdminSDHolder.

framework.name: ANSSI
items: since tombstone reanimation is an uncommon and highly privileged operation.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged objects with unprivileged owners
indicators.description: Looks for privileged objects (adminCount =1) that are owned by an unprivileged account. Any compromise of an unprivileged account could result in a privileged object’s delegation being modified.

indicators.indicatorName: Unprivileged users can add computer accounts to domain
indicators.description: Checks to see if unprivileged domain members are allowed to add computer accounts to a domain. Having the ability to add computer accounts to a domain can be abused by Kerberos-based attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Users with permissions to set Server Trust Account
indicators.description: Checks the domain NC head permissions to see if the Server_Trust_Account flag is set on computer objects. An attacker that can seed authenticated users with these permissions can utilize their access to promote any computer they control to Domain Controller status, enabling privilege escalation to AD services and carrying out credential access attacks such as DCSync.

indicators.indicatorName: AD Certificate Authority with Web Enrollment – ESC8
indicators.description: Identifies AD CS servers in the domain that accept NTLM authentication to Web Enrollment. Attackers may abuse a flaw in AD CS Web Enrollment that enables NTLM relay attacks to authenticate as a privileged user.

indicators.indicatorName: Anonymous access to Active Directory enabled
indicators.description: Looks for the presence of the flag that enables anonymous access. Anonymous access would allow unauthenticated users to query AD.

indicators.indicatorName: Anonymous NSPI access to AD enabled
indicators.description: Detects when anonymous name service provider interface (NSPI) access is enabled. Allows anonymous RPC-based binds to AD. NSPI is rarely enabled, so if it is found to be enabled it should be a cause for concern.

indicators.indicatorName: Certificate templates that allow requesters to specify a subjectAltName
indicators.description: Checks if certificate templates are enabling requesters to specify a subjectAltName in the CSR. When certificate templates allow requesters to specify a subjectAltName in the CSR, the result is that they can request a certificate as anyone (for example, a domain admin). When that is combined with an authentication EKU present in the certificate template, it can become extremely dangerous.

indicators.indicatorName: Certificate templates with 3 or more insecure configurations
indicators.description: Checks if certificate templates in the forest have a minimum of three insecure configurations: Manager approval is disabled, No authorized signatures are required, SAN enabled, Authentication EKU present. Each of these configurations can be exploited by adversaries to gain access.

indicators.indicatorName: Computers with older OS versions
indicators.description: Looks for machine accounts that are running versions of Windows older than Windows Server 2012 R2 and Windows 8.1. Computers running older and unsupported OS versions could be targeted with known or unpatched exploits.

indicators.indicatorName: Computers with password last set over 90 days ago
indicators.description: Looks for computer accounts that have not automatically rotated their passwords. Computer accounts should automatically rotate their passwords every 30 days; objects that are not doing this could show evidence of tampering.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous control paths expose certificate containers
indicators.description: Looks for non-default principals with permissions on the NTAuthCertificates container, which holds the intermediate CA certificates used to authenticate to Active Directory. Unprivileged users with permissions on the NTAuthCerticates container have the ability to escalate their access and make the domain trust a rogue CA.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous control paths expose certificate templates
indicators.description: Looks for non-default principals with the ability to write properties on a certificate template. Unprivileged users with write properties on certificate templates have the ability to escalate their access and create vulnerable certificates to enroll.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous Trust Attribute Set
indicators.description: Identifies trusts with either of the following attributes set: TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_ CROSS_ORGANIZATION_ENABLE_TGT_DELEGATION or TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_ PIM_TRUST. Setting these attributes will either allow a Kerberos ticket to be delegated or reduce the protection that SID filtering provides.

indicators.indicatorName: Domain controllers in an inconsistent state
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers that may be in an inconsistent state, indicating a possible rogue or otherwise non-functional DC. Illegitimate machines acting as DCs could indicate someone has compromised the environment (e.g., using DCShadow or similar DC spoofing attack).

indicators.indicatorName: Domain controllers that have not authenticated to the domain for more than 45 days
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers that have not authenticated to the domain in over 45 days. Lack of domain authentication reveals out-of-sync machines. If an attacker compromises an offline DC and cracks the credentials or re-connects to the domain, they may be able to introduce unwanted changes to Active Directory.

indicators.indicatorName: Domain controllers with old passwords
indicators.description: Looks for domain controller machine accounts whose password has not been reset in over 45 days. Machine accounts with older passwords could indicate a DC that is no longer functioning in the domain. In addition, DCs with older machine account passwords could be more easily taken over.

indicators.indicatorName: Domain trust to a third-party domain without quarantine
indicators.description: Looks for outbound forest trusts that have the Quarantine flag set to false. An attacker that has compromised the remote domain can create a “spoofable” account to gain access to every resource on the local domain. If a dangerous control path is exposed, any “spoofable” account could also escalate his privileges up to Domain Admins and compromise the entire forest.”

indicators.indicatorName: Domains with obsolete functional levels
indicators.description: Looks for AD domains that have a domain functional level set to Windows Server 2012 or lower. Lower functional levels mean that newer security features available in AD cannot be leveraged.

indicators.indicatorName: Evidence of Mimikatz DCShadow attack
indicators.description: Looks for evidence that a machine has been used to inject arbitrary changes into AD using a “fake” domain controller. These changes bypass the security event log and cannot be spotted using standard monitoring tools.

indicators.indicatorName: gMSA objects with old passwords
indicators.description: Looks for group managed service accounts (gMSA) that have not automatically rotated their passwords. Objects that are not rotating their passwords regularly could show evidence of tampering.

indicators.indicatorName: LDAP signing is not required on Domain Controllers
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers where LDAP signing is not required. Unsigned network traffic is exposed to MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacks, where attackers alter packets and forward them to the LDAP server, causing the server to make decisions based on forged requests from the LDAP client.

indicators.indicatorName: LLMNR enforced by GPO
indicators.description: Checks if any Group Policy Objects (GPOs) explicitly enforce Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) settings via registry policy entries. If LLMNR is not explicitly disabled in the environment, it creates an opportunity for attackers to perform LLMNR/NBNS poisoning attacks. These attacks can be used to intercept authentication requests and capture NTLMv2 hashes, which can then be cracked offline or used in relay attacks. This is a common tactic in lateral movement during internal network penetration tests and real-world breaches.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-standard schema permissions
indicators.description: Looks for additional principals with any permissions beyond generic Read to the schema partitions. By default, modification permissions on the schema are limited to Schema Admins. These permissions grant the trusted principal complete control over the Active Directory.

indicators.indicatorName: NTFRS SYSVOL replication
indicators.description: Looks for indication of usage of FRS for SYSVOL replication. NTFRS is an older protocol that has been replaced by DFSR. Attackers that can manipulate NTFRS vulnerabilities to compromise SYSVOL can potentially change GPOs and logon scripts to propagate malware and move laterally across the environment.

indicators.indicatorName: Operator groups no longer protected by AdminSDHolder and SDProp
indicators.description: Checks if dwAdminSDExMask on dsHeurstics has been set, which indicates a change to the SDProp behavior that could compromise security. A change to the AdminSDHolder SDProp behavior could indicate an attempt at defense evasion.

indicators.indicatorName: Outbound forest trust with SID History enabled
indicators.description: Looks for outbound forest trusts that have the TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_TREAT_AS_ EXTERNAL flag set to true. If this flag is set, a cross-forest trust to a domain is treated as an external trust for the purposes of SID filtering. This attribute relaxes the more stringent filtering performed on cross-forest trusts.

indicators.indicatorName: Print spooler service is enabled on a DC
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers that have the print spooler service running, which is enabled by default. Several critical flaws were found in Windows Print Spooler services, which directly affect Print spoolers installed on domain controllers, enabling remote code execution.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged user credentials cached on RODC
indicators.description: Looks for privileged users with credentials that are cached on RODCs. While not immediately indicative of an attack, privileged user accounts are sensitive and should not be cached on RODCs since their physical security is not as robust as a full DC.

indicators.indicatorName: Query policies that have the attribute of ldap deny list set
indicators.description: Checks for LDAP IP deny lists (ldapipdenylist attribute) across multiple domains in an AD environment. Unauthorized or unexpected entries in the LDAP IP deny list could suggest a security breach or an attempt to limit access to critical resources maliciously.

indicators.indicatorName: Risky RODC credential caching
indicators.description: Looks for a Password Replication Policy that allows privileged objects. If privileged users are in the allow list, they can be exposed to credential theft on an RODC.

indicators.indicatorName: Smart card password rotation disabled
indicators.description: Checks whether the mcDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts attribute is disabled. This attribute determines if smart card-only accounts must follow regular password rotation schedules. When this attribute is disabled, smart card-only accounts can maintain the same password indefinitely, which can potentially create a security vulnerability. This security feature is available in domains operating at Windows Server 2016 functional level or higher.

indicators.indicatorName: SMB Signing is not required on Domain Controllers
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers where SMB signing is not required. Unsigned network traffic is susceptible to attacks abusing the NTLM challenge-response protocol. A common example of such attacks is SMB Relay, where an attacker is positioned between the client and the server in order to capture data packets transmitted between the two, thus gaining unauthorized access to the server or other servers on the network.

indicators.indicatorName: SMBv1 is enabled on Domain Controllers
indicators.description: Looks for domain controllers where SMBv1 protocol is enabled. SMBv1 is an old protocol (deprecated by Microsoft in 2014), which is considered unsafe and susceptible to all kinds of attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Unexpected accounts in Cert Publishers Group
indicators.description: Checks to see if the Cert Publishers Group contains members that aren’t expected to be there. Individuals belonging to the Cert Publishers Group have the ability to introduce a potentially harmful Certificate Authority (CA) within an ADCS environment that will be trusted by all clients.

indicators.indicatorName: Unsecured DNS configuration
indicators.description: Looks for DNS zones configure with ZONE_UPDATE_UNSECURE, which allows updating a DSN record anonymously. An attacker could leverage this exposure to add a new DSN record or replace an existing DNS record to spoof a management interface, then wait for incoming connections in order to steal credentials.

indicators.indicatorName: Weak certificate cipher
indicators.description: Looks for certificates stored in Active Directory with keysize smaller than 2048 bits or using DSA encryption. Weak certificates can be abused by attackers to gain access to systems who use certificate authentication.

indicators.indicatorName: Well-known privileged SIDs in sIDHistory
indicators.description: Looks for security principals that contain specific SIDs of accounts from built-in privileged groups within the sIDHistory attribute. Allows those security principals to have the same privileges as those privileged accounts, but in a way that is not obvious to monitor (e.g., through group membership).

indicators.indicatorName: Zerologon vulnerability
indicators.description: Looks for security vulnerability to CVE-2020-1472, which was patched by Microsoft in August 2020. Without this patch, an unauthenticated attacker can exploit CVE-2020-1472 to elevate their privileges and get administrative access on the domain.

indicators.indicatorName: Administrative units are not being used
indicators.description: Checks for the use of administrative units in the Entra tenant. Administrative units are an Entra ID feature that allow for restricting administrative scope of privileged users. Organizations that leverage administrative units can have more granularity in role assignment.

indicators.indicatorName: Application expired secrets and certificates
indicators.description: Checks for certificates or secrets that have reached their expiration dates. This indicator does not indicate a direct risk or likelihood of compromise.

indicators.indicatorName: Application instance property lock disabled
indicators.description: This indicator checks for applications that have the application instance property lock disabled. Application instance property lock is a feature in Entra ID that restricts the ability to add or modify sensitive properties on service principals. Attackers can look for privileged service principals and attempt to use them to move laterally by adding credentials to the existing service principal if they gain access to a user with the ability to do so.

indicators.indicatorName: Application Name and Geographic Location additional contexts are disabled on MFA
indicators.description: Checks if the application name and geographic location additional contexts are disabled on multi-factor authentication (MFA). Enabling the application name and geographic location additional contexts on MFA provides an additional level of security for a user sign-in.

indicators.indicatorName: Certificate-Based Authentication Persistence
indicators.description: Assesses the presence of specific Entra ID Microsoft graph app roles and permissions, that when combined can enable a user to establish persistence through certificate-based authentication (CBA).

indicators.indicatorName: Check for guests having permission to invite other guests
indicators.description: Check for guest invite permissions. It is not recommended to allow guests to send guest invitations. o prevent unauthorized guests from inviting others into the organization, consider updating the “Guest invite settings” to restrict this ability.

indicators.indicatorName: Check for risky API permissions granted to application service principals
indicators.description: Checks for API permissions that could be risky if not properly planned and approved. Malicious application administrators could use these permissions to grant administrative privileges to themselves or others.

indicators.indicatorName: Check for users with weak or no MFA
indicators.description: Checks all users for multi-factor authentication (MFA) registration and the methods configured. Due to the lack of uniform security measures within mobile networks, SMS and Voice are considered less secure than mobile applications and FIDO. A malicious user can vish/smish codes and trick users into providing authentication.

indicators.indicatorName: Check if legacy authentication is allowed
indicators.description: Checks whether legacy authentication is blocked, either using conditional access policies or security defaults. Allowing legacy authentication increases the risk that an attacker will logon using previously compromised credentials.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access policies contain private IP addresses
indicators.description: Checks if any Conditional Access policies contain named locations with private IP addresses. Having private IP addresses in named locations associated with Conditional Access policies could result in an undesired security posture.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access policies that contain MFA Trusted IPs
indicators.description: Checks if any enabled Conditional Access policies contain references to MFA Trusted IPs. MFA Trusted IPs is a legacy mechanism originally designed for specifying IP addresses to exclude from per-user MFA. Organizations should review the MFA Trusted IPs settings to determine if the desired addresses can be created as Named Locations.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access Policy does not require MFA on privileged accounts
indicators.description: Checks whether Conditional Access policies require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for privileged accounts. Users who hold privileged roles in Entra ID are high-value targets for an attacker. It is critical for organizations to require MFA for all users holding privileged roles.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access Policy that disables admin token persistence
indicators.description: Looks for Conditional Access policies that disable token persistence for users with admin roles and have a sign-in frequency that is less than or equal to nine hours. When an admin login has their token cached on the client, they are vulnerable for a Primary Refresh Token related attack.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access Policy that does not require a password change from high risk users
indicators.description: Checks whether a Conditional Access policy exists that requires a password change if the user is determined to be high risk by the Entra ID Identity Protection user risk API. A high user risk represents a high probability that an account has been compromised.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access Policy that does not require MFA when sign-in risk has been identified
indicators.description: Checks whether a Conditional Access policy exists that requires MFA if the authentication request risk is determined to be medium or high by the Entra ID. Identity Protection sign-in risk API. A medium or high sign-in risk represents a medium to high probability that an unauthorized authentication request was made.

indicators.indicatorName: Conditional Access policy with Continuous Access Evaluation disabled
indicators.description: Checks for Conditional Access policies that have the Continuous Access Evaluation feature disabled. The Continuous Access Evaluation feature allows you to revoke the access token for Microsoft applications and limit the time an attacker has access to company data.

indicators.indicatorName: Custom banned password protection not in use
indicators.description: Checks if custom banned password protection is enabled in Entra ID. Custom banned password protection allows organizations to specify customer banned words, helping to prevent users from creating weak passwords that may contain words relative to the organization.

indicators.indicatorName: Custom role assigned to unprivileged principals in an app’s scope
indicators.description: Identifies cases where a privileged custom role is assigned to an unprivileged user or service principal, scoped to a specific application. Assigning a privileged custom role to an unprivileged principal within the scope of a specific application can introduce a stealthy privilege escalation vector. These assignments are often overlooked because they do not involve built-in directory roles, making them harder to detect through standard RBAC reviews.

indicators.indicatorName: Detect MFA policy changes for groups and users
indicators.description: Looks for changes (removal of users and groups) from MFA policies. MFA policies are considered a sensitive asset in the identity security of the organization. In cases of changes in membership of users and groups in MFA policies, there may be a malicious compromise of users.

indicators.indicatorName: Dynamic administrative units with self-assignment risk
indicators.description: Detects cases where a user assigned to manage a dynamic administrative unit (AU) also has permissions to modify the attribute(s) used to determine AU membership. Entra ID supports dynamic AUs, where user membership is automatically determined by property-based rules such as department or job title. If this is misconfigured, this setup can be abused to bypass scoping restrictions and escalate privileges.

indicators.indicatorName: Ensure all non-privileged users can complete MFA
indicators.description: Checks for non-privileged users that cannot complete the MFA process based on the authentication details they enter. MFA adds an extra layer of security to the sign-in process, which helps protect your organization against security breaches. Users who use MFA are less likely to fall victim to phishing attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Enterprise applications using SAML for SSO
indicators.description: Checks for enterprise applications (service principals) in Entra ID configured to use SAML for SSO. Applications using SAML can be prone to Silver SAML, a type of SAML response forging, if an attacker is able to obtain the signing certificate used by Entra ID.

indicators.indicatorName: Entra Connect sync account password reset
indicators.description: Checks for Conditional Access policies that have the Continuous Access Evaluation feature disabled. The Continuous Access Evaluation feature allows you to revoke the access token for Microsoft applications and limit the time an attacker has access to company data.

indicators.indicatorName: Entra custom Roles with risky permissions
indicators.description: Checks if a custom role contains risky permissions. Potentially, custom roles can be used to gain access to sensitive information or perform malicious actions.

indicators.indicatorName: Entra tenant is susceptible to Hidden Consent Grant attack
indicators.description: Checks app permissions and settings to determine if the Entra tenant is susceptible to Hidden Consent Grant attacks. A Hidden Consent Grant attack is a type of phishing attack where a malicious actor who controls an application with Directory.ReadWrite.All permissions gains access to an application and exploits granted permissions to escalate his privileges.

indicators.indicatorName: FIDO2 Attestation is not enforced
indicators.description: Checks if FIDO2 security key attestation is enforced in Entra ID. FIDO2 security key attestation provides assurance during key registration that a key is a specific make and model. If FIDO2 enforcement is disabled, there is a lower level of assurance of the key being registered

indicators.indicatorName: Global Administrators that signed in during the last 14 days
indicators.description: Looks for Global Administrators that have signed in during the past 14 days. Users that hold the Global Administrator role are the most privileged users in Entra ID. An attacker will find users with the Global Administrator role as high-valued, and a compromised Global Administrator can lead to several attacks against the organization.

indicators.indicatorName: Guest accounts that were inactive for more than 30 days
indicators.description: Checks for guest accounts that have not signed in, using an interactive or non-interactive sign in, during the past 30 days. Inactive guest accounts leave an open gate to your Azure tenant.

indicators.indicatorName: Guest invites not accepted in last 30 days
indicators.description: Checks for guest invites that were not accepted within 30 days of the invitation. Stale guest invitations pose a security risk and should be deleted.

indicators.indicatorName: Guest users are not restricted
indicators.description: Checks guest users are restricted in the tenant. Attackers may use unrestricted guest users to perform enumeration of users and groups in the tenant.

indicators.indicatorName: Hybrid-synced privileged role accounts
indicators.description: Detects privileged role accounts (excluding Global Administrators) that are synchronized from on-premises Active Directory. According to Microsoft’s security guidance, privileged role accounts should be cloud-only to minimize exposure and prevent compromise through on-premises infrastructure.

indicators.indicatorName: Less than 2 Global Administrators exist
indicators.description: Checks for the presence of less than two Global Administrators. This indicator aligns with Microsoft recommendations that customers should have at least two Global Administrators in the tenant.

indicators.indicatorName: List of risky users (medium or high level)
indicators.description: Checks for risky users in the tenant with medium or high level of risk. Risky users are individuals or accounts exhibiting behaviors increasing the likelihood of security incidents or breaches, such as weak authentication practices, susceptibility to phishing, unusual activity patterns, accessing resources from unsecured devices or networks, or holding elevated privileges. These users pose significant risks, potentially leading to credential compromises, data breaches, or insider threats.

indicators.indicatorName: MFA bombing attack occurred in the past day
indicators.description: Monitors user login activity to detect MFA bombing attempts on privileged accounts. It looks for unusual patterns in login activity of more than five failed MFA attempts within the last day. Note that this indicator will not detect activity of users using passwordless authentication. MFA bombing is a tactic where an attacker spams the user with MFA requests, and the user unknowingly or unwillingly accepts the request.

indicators.indicatorName: MFA not configured for privileged accounts
indicators.description: Checks whether Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) is enabled for users with administrative rights. Accounts with privileged access are more vulnerable targets to attackers. A compromise of a privileged user represents a significant risk and therefore requires extra protection.

indicators.indicatorName: More than 10 Privileged Administrators exist
indicators.description: Checks for the presence of 10 or more Privileged Assigned Roles. This indicator aligns with Microsoft recommendations that customers have no more than 10 privileged role assignments.

indicators.indicatorName: More than 5 Global Administrators exist
indicators.description: Checks for the presence of five or more Global Administrators. Global Administrators control your Azure AD environment and have access to all administrative features and full control of Azure AD.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-admin users can create tenants
indicators.description: Checks if non-admin users are allowed to create Entra tenants. By default, all users are allowed to create additional Entra tenants from an existing Entra tenant. Organizations should restrict non-admin users from creating tenants.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-admin users can register custom applications
indicators.description: Checks for an authorization policy that enables non-admin users to register custom applications. If non-admin users are allowed to register custom-developed enterprise applications, attackers might use that loophole to register nefarious applications, which they can then leverage to gain additional permissions.

indicators.indicatorName: Non-synced Entra user that is eligible for a privileged role
indicators.description: Checks for Entra ID users that are eligible for a high-privilege role and have the proxyAddress attribute but are not synchronized with an AD account. An attacker might use SMTP matching to synchronize controlled AD users with Entra users that are eligible for high-privilege roles. This process overwrites the AAD password and could result in privilege escalation over AAD.

indicators.indicatorName: Permanent active privileged role assignment
indicators.description: Checks for the presence of permanent active privileged role assignments. Privileged roles in Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) that are assigned as “permanently active” pose significant security risks. This configuration allows users continuous access to elevated privileges, increasing the risk of privilege escalation and potential exploitation.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged accounts with mailbox
indicators.description: Searches for privileged accounts in the Entra tenant that have an associated mailbox. Privileged accounts in the tenant that have a mailbox may be prime targets for attackers. Attackers may try to use the mailbox address of privileged users to achieve tokens to gain access, obtain sensitive data, or move laterally through the environment.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged group contains guest account
indicators.description: Checks whether any privileged roles have been assigned to guest accounts. External attackers covet privileged accounts, as they provide a fast track to an organization’s most critical systems. Guest accounts represent an external entity that does not undergo the same security as users in your tenant; therefore, assigning privileged roles to them poses a heightened risk.

indicators.indicatorName: Prohibited Entra ID roles assigned
indicators.description: Checks for the assignment of roles in Entra ID that are deprecated or prohibited from use. Deprecated roles or roles marked as “never use” can pose significant security risks if assigned. These roles may have unintended permissions or may not be properly maintained, potentially leading to security vulnerabilities.

indicators.indicatorName: Report suspicious MFA activity disabled
indicators.description: Checks the “Report suspicious activity” authentication method setting. Enabling the “Report suspicious activity” setting allows users to report suspicious MFA activity, which can help organizations detect social engineering attacks such as MFA fatigue.

indicators.indicatorName: s Directory Synchronization Accounts role member
indicators.description: Checks for users who are assigned the Directory Synchronization Accounts role that are not the default Entra Connect users. The Directory Synchronization Accounts role in Entra ID is reserved for accounts used for Entra Connect. This directory role is highly privileged and is not meant for assignment to users

indicators.indicatorName: Security defaults not enabled
indicators.description: When there are no conditional access policies configured, this indicator checks whether security defaults are enabled. It is recommended that security defaults be used for tenants that have no conditional access policies configured. Security defaults will require MFA, block legacy authentication, and require additional authentication when accessing the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, and the Azure CLI.

indicators.indicatorName: Security questions are in use
indicators.description: Checks if security questions are being used for Entra self-service password reset. Security questions, also known as knowledge-based authentication (KBA), can be used for authentication flows during a self-service password reset scenario. Organizations that rely on KBA as a means of authentication for self-service password reset are at a greater risk of an attacker using this to compromise users

indicators.indicatorName: Self-service password reset enabled for privileged roles
indicators.description: Checks whether users in privileged roles in Entra ID can use self-service password reset. Self-service password reset (SSPR) is beneficial in organizations for end users but has security trade-offs for privileged accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: Suspicious credentials on Microsoft service principals
indicators.description: Checks if certain Microsoft service principals have secrets assigned to them. In Entra ID it is possible to assign credentials such as secrets or keys to service principals for Microsoft applications. In certain scenarios, this would then allow you to act with the same rights the application has using OAuth 2.0 client credential grant flows against Microsoft Graph API.

indicators.indicatorName: Unprivileged owner of a privileged group
indicators.description: Checks for the presence of an unprivileged owner of a group with privileged roles. Assigning roles to a group instead of individual principals streamlines the process of adding or removing users and ensures consistent permissions for all group members. However, group owner can add themselves to the group at any time, posing a privilege escalation risk if the owner is an unprivileged principal.

indicators.indicatorName: Unresolved Entra ID privileged role members
indicators.description: Identifies privileged role assignments where the member cannot be found, either due to deleted eligible users or hidden GDAP partner relationships. Deleted eligible users that remain in role assignments can create confusion and complicate role management. GDAP partner relationships, while legitimate, need to be properly tracked and managed to maintain security oversight.

indicators.indicatorName: Unrestricted user consent allowed
indicators.description: Checks if users are allowed to add application from unverified publishers. When users are allowed to consent to any third-party applications, there is considerable risk that an allowed application will take intrusive or risky actions.

indicators.indicatorName: User consent is allowed for risky applications
indicators.description: Checks for an Entra ID authorization policy that allows users to grant consent for risky applications. To enhance security, it is recommended to set the allowUserConsentForRiskyApps property to false. This prevents users from granting consent to risky applications independently.

indicators.indicatorName: Users are not using their privileged roles
indicators.description: Checks for users who have not activated a role assigned to them for over 30 days. Users holding excessive privileges that are not used expand an organization’s attack surface area.

indicators.indicatorName: Users can create security groups
indicators.description: Checks if non-admin users can create security groups. By default, users can create security groups in the Entra tenant. Entra ID does not require unique group names, and an attacker may create malicious security groups with duplicate names of valid groups, in an effort to have the malicious group assigned further privileges

indicators.indicatorName: Users or devices inactive for at least 90 days
indicators.description: Checks for users or devices that have not signed in during the past 90 days. Users or devices that have been inactive for 90 days or more are likely no longer in use and leave an open gate to the Azure AD tenant.

indicators.indicatorName: Changes to Default Domain Policy or Default Domain Controllers Policy in the last 7 days
indicators.description: Looks for recent changes to the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controllers Policy GPOs. These GPOs control domain-wide and domain controller-wide security settings and can be misused to gain privileged access to AD.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous GPO logon script path
indicators.description: Looks for logon script paths to scripts that do not exist and where a low-privileged user has permissions on their parent folder. It also checks for logon script paths to existing scripts that give less-privileged users permissions to modify the script. By inserting a new script or changing an existing script that gives a normal user permission to change the script or access to their parent folder, an attacker can remotely run code on a larger part of the network without special privileges.

indicators.indicatorName: Dangerous user rights granted by GPO
indicators.description: Looks for non-privileged users who are granted elevated permissions through GPO. An attacker can potentially exploit the user rights granted by a GPO to gain access to systems, steal sensitive information, or cause other types of damage.

indicators.indicatorName: GPO linking delegation at the AD Site level
indicators.description: Looks for non-privileged principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DACL/Write Owner on the object. When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the AD Site level, they have the ability to effect change on domain controllers. They can potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture.

indicators.indicatorName: GPO linking delegation at the domain controller OU level
indicators.description: Looks for non-privileged principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DAC/Write Owner on the object. When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the domain controller OU level, they have the ability to effect change on domain controllers. They can potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture.

indicators.indicatorName: GPO linking delegation at the domain level
indicators.description: Looks for non-privileged principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DACL/Write Owner on the object. When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the domain level, they have the ability to effect change across all users and computers in the domain. They can potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture.

indicators.indicatorName: GPO Weak LM Hash storage enabled
indicators.description: Detects when the “Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change” Group Policy Object setting is disabled within the Windows operating system. When this setting is disabled, LAN Manager (LM) hashes, which are vulnerable to password cracking techniques, continue to be stored during password changes. Enabling this setting strengthens security by preventing the storage of weak LM hashes and prompting the use of stronger password storage mechanisms.

indicators.indicatorName: GPO with scheduled tasks configured
indicators.description: When a scheduled task launches an executable, this indicator checks to see if low privilege users have permissions to modify GPOs. Scheduled tasks configured through group policies can be risky if not set up correctly. They can cause unintended problems and potential security vulnerabilities.

indicators.indicatorName: Reversible passwords found in GPOs
indicators.description: Looks in the SYSVOL for GPOs that contain passwords that can be easily decrypted by an attacker (so-called “Cpassword” entries). This area is one of the first things attackers look for when they’ve gained access to an AD environment.

indicators.indicatorName: SYSVOL Executable Changes
indicators.description: Looks for modifications to executable files within SYSVOL. Changes to the executable files within SYSVOL should be accounted for or investigated to look for potential security posture weakening.

indicators.indicatorName: Writable shortcuts found in GPO
indicators.description: Looks for shortcuts within Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that are writable by low privileged users. When low privileged users have the ability to modify shortcuts within GPOs, it could potentially lead to security risks and unauthorized modifications.

indicators.indicatorName: AAD privileged users that are also privileged in AD
indicators.description: Checks for Azure AD privileged users that are also privileged users in on-premises AD. A compromise of an account that is privileged in both AD and AAD can result in both environments being compromised.

indicators.indicatorName: Accounts with Kerberos constrained delegation configured to SSO computer account
indicators.description: Looks for accounts that have constrained delegation configured to the SSO computer account, AZUREADSSOACC. If an account in Active Directory has Kerberos constrained delegation configured to the AZUREADSSOACC computer account, an attacker can use this to generate Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets

indicators.indicatorName: AD privileged users that are synced to AAD
indicators.description: Checks for AD privileged users that are synchronized to AAD. When a privileged AD user is synchronized to AAD, a compromise of the AAD user can result in the on-premises environment being compromised as well.

indicators.indicatorName: Password hash synchronization is not enabled
indicators.description: Checks whether password hash synchronization is enabled in the Entra tenant. Password hash synchronization is used to sync user password hashes from an on-premise Active Directory instance to a cloud-based Entra ID instance. This synchronization helps protect against leaked credentials being replayed from previous attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: RC4 or DES encryption is supported by SSO computer account
indicators.description: Checks if RC4 or DES encryption is supported by the SSO computer account, AZUREADSSOACC. RC4 and DES are considered insecure forms of encryption and are susceptible to various cryptographic attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Resource Based Constrained Delegation applied to AZUREADSSOACC account
indicators.description: Looks for Resource Based Constrained Delegation configured for the Azure SSO account, AZUREADSSOACC. An account with Resource Based Constrained Delegation would allow that principal to generate a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) request to the Azure tenant on behalf of the AZUREADSSOACC account as any user and impersonate that user.

indicators.indicatorName: SSO computer account with password last set over 90 days ago
indicators.description: Checks the Azure SSO computer account (AZUREADSSOACC) to determine if the password has been rotated in the last 90 days. The password for the Azure SSO computer account is not automatically changed every 30 days. If the password for this account is compromised, an attacker could generate a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) request to the AZUREADSSOACC account as any user, which has the effect of generating a ticket to Azure and impersonating that user.

indicators.indicatorName: Accounts with altSecurityIdentities configured
indicators.description: Checks for accounts with the altSecurityIdentities attribute configured. The altSecurityIdentities attribute is a multi-valued attribute used to create mappings for X.509 certificates and external Kerberos accounts. When configured, it is possible to add values that essentially impersonate that account.

indicators.indicatorName: Accounts with Constrained Delegation configured to ghost SPN
indicators.description: Looks for accounts that have Constrained Delegation configured to ghost SPNs. When computers are decommissioned, their delegation configuration is not always cleaned up. Such a delegation could allow an attacker that has the privileges to write to the ServicePrincipalName attribute of another service account, to escalate privileges on those services.

indicators.indicatorName: Accounts with Constrained Delegation configured to krbtgt
indicators.description: Looks for accounts that have Constrained Delegation configured to the krbtgt service. Creating a Kerberos delegation to the krbtgt account itself allows that principal (user or computer) to generate a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) request to the krbtgt account as any user, which has the effect of generating a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) similar to a Golden Ticket.

indicators.indicatorName: Computer account takeover through Kerberos Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)
indicators.description: Looks for the msDS-Allowed-ToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on computer objects. Attackers could use Kerberos RBCD configuration to escalate privileges through a computer they control if that computer has delegation to the target system.

indicators.indicatorName: Computer or user accounts with SPN that have unconstrained delegation
indicators.description: Looks for computer or user accounts with SPN that are trusted for unconstrained Kerberos delegation. These accounts store users’ Kerberos TGT locally to authenticate to other systems on their behalf. Computers and users trusted with unconstrained delegation are easily targeted for Kerberos-based attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Domain controllers with Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) enabled
indicators.description: Detects a configuration that grants certain accounts with complete delegation to domain controllers.

indicators.indicatorName: Kerberos krbtgt account with old password
indicators.description: Looks for a krbtgt user account whose password has not changed in the past 180 days. If the krbtgt account’s password is compromised, Golden Ticket attacks can be performed to obtain access to any resource in an AD domain.

indicators.indicatorName: Kerberos protocol transition delegation configured
indicators.description: Looks for services that have been configured to allow Kerberos protocol transition, which basically says that a delegated service can use any available authentication protocol. Compromised services can reduce the quality of their authentication protocol that is more easily compromised (e.g., NTLM).

indicators.indicatorName: krbtgt account with Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) enabled
indicators.description: Looks for a krbtgt account that has Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) defined. Normally, delegations should not be created on the krbtgt account; if found, they could represent significant risk and should be mitigated quickly.

indicators.indicatorName: Objects with constrained delegation configured
indicators.description: Looks for any objects that have values in the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute (i.e., constrained delegation) and does not have the UserAccountControl bit for protocol transition set. Attackers may use delegations to move laterally or escalate privileges if they compromise a service that is trusted to delegate.

indicators.indicatorName: Primary users with SPN not supporting AES encryption on Kerberos
indicators.description: Shows all primary users with servicePrincipalNames (SPNs) that do not support AES-128 or AES-256 encryption type. AES encryption is stronger than RC4 encryption. Configuring primary users with SPNs that support AES encryption will not mitigate attacks such as kerberoasting. However, it does force AES encryption by default, meaning that it is possible to monitor for encryption downgrade attacks to RC4 (kerberoasting attacks).

indicators.indicatorName: Principals with constrained authentication delegation enabled for a DC service
indicators.description: Looks for computers and users that have constrained delegation enabled for a service running on a DC. If an attacker can create such a delegation, they can authenticate to that service using any user that is not protected against delegation.

indicators.indicatorName: Principals with constrained delegation using protocol transition enabled for a DC service
indicators.description: Looks for computers and users that have constrained delegation using protocol transition defined against a service running on a DC. If an attacker can create such a delegation for a service that they can control or compromise an existing service, they can effectively gain a TGS for any user with privileges to the DC.

indicators.indicatorName: Privileged users with ServicePrincipalNames defined
indicators.description: Looks for accounts with the adminCount attribute set to 1 AND ServicePrincipalNames (SPNs) defined on the account. Privileged accounts that have an SPN defined are targets for Kerberos-based attacks that can elevate privileges to those accounts.

indicators.indicatorName: RC4 or DES encryption type is supported by Domain Controllers
indicators.description: Checks if RC4 or DES encryption is supported by domain controllers. RC4 and DES are considered an insecure form of encryption, susceptible to various cryptographic attacks. Multiple vulnerabilities in the RC4 or DES algorithm allow MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) and deciphering attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: Users with ServicePrincipalName defined
indicators.description: Provides a way to visually inventory all user accounts that have ServicePrincipalNames (SPNs) defined. Generally, SPNs are only defined for “Kerberized” services; other accounts with an SPN may be cause for concern.

indicators.indicatorName: Users with the attribute userPassword set
indicators.description: Checks if the userPassword attribute exists on accounts. The userPassword attribute saves passwords in clear text and can be queried using LDAP, which can potentially expose passwords.

indicators.indicatorName: Write access to RBCD on DC
indicators.description: Looks for users who are not in Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or Built-in Admins groups that have write access on Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) for domain controllers. Attackers that can gain write access to RBCD for a resource can cause the resource to impersonate any user (except where delegation is explicitly disallowed).

indicators.indicatorName: Write access to RBCD on krbtgt account
indicators.description: Looks for users who are not in Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or Built-in Admins groups that have write access on Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) for the krbtgt account. Attackers that can gain write access to RBCD for a resource can cause the resource to impersonate any user (except where delegation is explicitly disallowed).

indicators.indicatorName: High privileged custom roles
indicators.description: Checks for custom roles that grant elevated privileges to allow a user to perform actions on other users’ passwords and MFA. Custom roles grant elevated privileges and potentially pose a significant security risk if not properly managed.

indicators.indicatorName: New API token was created
indicators.description: Checks if a new API token has been created in the last 7 days. API tokens with high privileges allow unauthorized access and actions in Okta. If an attacker gains access to the token’s password, they can leverage it to query and perform actions potentially leading to persistence and compromising the environment.

indicators.indicatorName: New permission has been granted to a group
indicators.description: Checks if any permissions have been granted to a group in the last 7 days. Members of a group with high privileges can perform significant actions in Okta. Therefore, it is important to know which groups grant strong privileges.

indicators.indicatorName: New permission has been granted to user
indicators.description: Checks if any permissions have been granted to a user in the last 7 days. Users with high privileges can perform significant actions in Okta. Therefore, it is important to identify and monitor users who have been granted elevated privileges to mitigate the risk of unauthorized access and potential misuse of sensitive data.

indicators.indicatorName: New Super Admin permission has been granted to user
indicators.description: Checks for users who were granted “Super Admin” permissions in the last 7 days. Users with “Super Admin” privileges have extensive privileges and control over critical aspects of the Okta environment. Unauthorized or excessive granting of the “Super Admin” permission can significantly increase the risk of compromise and unauthorized access to Okta.

indicators.indicatorName: New Super Admin permissions has been granted to a group
indicators.description: Checks for groups where “Super Admin” permissions have been granted in the last 7 days. Members in a group with “Super Admin” privileges have extensive access and can perform significant actions in Okta. Therefore, it is important to closely monitor and control which groups are granted these strong privileges to prevent unauthorized access and potential compromise of the Okta environment.

indicators.indicatorName: Password policy check
indicators.description: Evaluates all password policies and verifies they adhere to Okta’s recommendations. A strong password policy is crucial in preventing unauthorized access to the environment through brute force attacks.

indicators.indicatorName: User activation in the last 7 days
indicators.description: Checks for users who were activated in the past 7 days. Activated users have the ability to authenticate and perform actions within the Okta environment. Therefore, it is important to monitor and verify the activation status of users to ensure that only authorized individuals have access.

indicators.indicatorName: User deactivation in the last 7 days
indicators.description: Checks for users who were deactivated in the past 7 days. Deactivated users no longer have the ability to authenticate and perform actions within the Okta environment. However, an attacker may intentionally deactivate a user to disrupt the functioning of the environment or to hide their activities. It is important to monitor and verify the deactivation status of users to ensure it aligns with the intended access controls.

indicators.indicatorName: Users without Multi- Factor Authentication (MFA)
indicators.description: Checks all users to identity those who have not registered for Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Users who are not configured with MFA are at a high risk of being compromised. This poses a significant threat not only to the user but also the entire environment.
